It’s about understanding what’s already going wrong. Press enter or click to view image in full size Introduction Imagine opening a shopping app to buy a pair of shoes. You search for the product, find the one you like, select your size, and add it to your cart. Everything seems fine until you reach checkout. The process is confusing. The delivery charges appear unexpectedly, and you have to fill in too many details. Eventually, you close the app and decide to buy from somewhere else. Now imagine that the same app launches five new features the following month. It introduces product recommendations, a wishlist, a loyalty program, a new home screen, and an AI shopping assistant. Sounds like progress, right? But what if customers are still leaving at checkout? The app has more features, but the original problem hasn’t changed. This is something that makes product management interesting to me. Building something new is exciting, but building something that genuinely solves a problem is much more important. The Problem With Always Wanting to Add More When we think about improving a product, our first instinct is often to add something. Users request new features. Competitors launch something interesting. Teams come up with creative ideas. Before long, the product roadmap becomes a long list of things to build. But there is one important question we sometimes forget to ask: Does the user actually need this, or does it just sound like a good idea? A feature might look impressive during a presentation. It might even attract attention when it launches. But if it doesn’t solve a real user problem, its long-term value may be limited. Think about a note-taking app. Suppose users complain that they struggle to find their old notes. The team could introduce AI summaries, colorful themes, and more customization options. These might be useful additions, but they don’t directly solve the problem users are facing. Improving search, adding filters, or organizing notes more effectively might have a much greater impact. The difference is simple: one approach focuses on adding features, while the other focuses on removing frustration. And that difference matters. Great Products Start With Understanding People A product is not successful simply because its team worked hard to build it. It becomes valuable when people find it useful enough to keep coming back. That requires understanding how people actually use it. What are they trying to achieve? Where do they get stuck? What makes them leave? What do they expect the product to do? These questions may not sound as exciting as discussing a new feature, but they often lead to better decisions. For example, imagine an online learning platform where many users stop watching after the second or third video. The obvious response might be to add more courses, introduce badges, or launch a leaderboard. But before building anything, the product team should understand why users are leaving. Perhaps the videos are too long. Maybe the content becomes difficult to follow. Some learners might not understand what to study next, while others may struggle to find time to complete a lesson. Each explanation points toward a different solution. If videos are too long, shorter lessons might help. If learners feel lost, a clearer learning path could make a difference. If motivation is the problem, progress tracking or reminders might be worth testing. The important thing is not to guess the solution before understanding the problem. Good product decisions begin with curiosity, not assumptions. More Features Can Sometimes Make a Product Worse We often associate progress with growth. More features, more options, more customization, and more functionality can make a product appear more advanced. But every new feature comes with a cost. It requires development time, testing, maintenance, and ongoing support. It can also make the user experience more complicated. Think about a simple mobile app that initially does one thing really well. Over time, the team adds multiple menus, settings, notifications, and secondary features. Eventually, users have to work harder to complete the same task they could once finish in a few seconds. The team may see the additional functionality as improvement. Users may see it as unnecessary complexity. This doesn’t mean that adding features is bad. New features can create real value when they address meaningful needs. The problem is assuming that every new feature automatically makes the product better. Sometimes, removing an unnecessary step or simplifying an existing experience can create more value than launching something new. A product manager needs to recognize that difference. Instead of asking only, “Can we build this?”, we should also ask, “Why should we build this?” Let’s return to the shopping app example. Suppose the team discovers that many users abandon their carts because delivery charges appear too late in the checkout process.
